topics.title: Pressure Injuries: Overview, Causes & Risk Factors
topics.summary: Prolonged pressure over a bony prominence cuts off blood flow long enough for tissue to die — and certain clients (immobile, malnourished, incontinent, confused, numb, febrile, older, chronically ill) are far more likely to get there.

sections.heading: What a pressure injury is
sections.body: A pressure injury is localized damage to the skin and underlying tissue caused by prolonged pressure, which decreases blood flow to the area. It may also result from friction or shearing forces. Other names: bedsore, pressure ulcer, decubitus ulcer. Incidence is up to about 29% in hospitals and 2.6–24% in long-term care; home-care cases are likely underreported and are an increasing concern.
bullets: Pathway: prolonged pressure → ↓ blood flow → ischemia → tissue necrosis → ulcer.
Most common over bony prominences: heels, sacrum, hips (greater trochanters), and ischia (ischial tuberosities).
Capillary pressure is about 32 mm Hg; external pressure above this, if sustained, closes off blood flow.

sections.heading: Friction and shear
bullets: Shear — the skin stays fixed to the sheet while the deeper tissue and skeleton slide (e.g., a client slides down in bed with the HOB raised). It stretches and tears deep blood vessels. Keeping the HOB at 30° or lower reduces shear.
Friction — the skin rubs against a surface (e.g., dragging a client up in bed), scraping the outer layer. Prevent it with draw sheets or lifts — never drag.

sections.heading: Risk factors (slides)
bullets: Immobility — paralysis, weakness, pain, sedation.
Inadequate nutrition — ↓ protein, calories, zinc, vitamin C → weight loss, muscle atrophy, edema; less padding over bone.
Incontinence — moisture, enzymes, and urea → maceration, skin breakdown, infection.
Decreased mental status — less able to sense or respond to pain or pressure.
Diminished sensation — paralysis, stroke, neuropathy, aging → the client cannot feel early warning signs.
Excessive body heat (fever) — ↑ metabolic rate and oxygen demand → worsens ischemia under pressure.
Advanced age — thinner, less elastic skin; ↓ oil; ↓ circulation; ↑ dryness.
Chronic medical conditions — diabetes and cardiovascular disease cause poor circulation and delayed healing.
Other contributing factors — poor lifting/transferring techniques, incorrect positioning, hard support surfaces, incorrect use of pressure-relieving devices.

sections.heading: Risk assessment tools
sections.body: Perform a baseline risk assessment with a validated tool such as the Braden scale (or Norton scale). The Braden scale has six subscales: sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition (each scored 1–4), and friction & shear (scored 1–3). Totals range from 6 to 23, and the lower the score, the higher the risk. Use the subscales to target care — a single subscale score of 1 is a problem even when the total looks reassuring.

pearls: Braden runs "backwards": a LOW score means HIGH risk.
Ask four questions: Can the client feel it? Move away from it? Is the skin wet? Is the client well nourished?
HOB up + sliding down = sacral shear.
Fever counts as a risk factor — it raises the tissue's oxygen demand.
redFlags: Any new nonblanchable redness over a bony prominence — reposition off it and reassess.
A sudden drop in Braden score (after sedation, surgery, or new incontinence) — step up the prevention plan the same shift.

topics.title: Pressure Injury Prevention: Nutrition, Skin Hygiene, Repositioning & Devices
topics.summary: Most pressure injuries are preventable: feed the tissue, keep the skin clean and dry, move the client on schedule without dragging, and use support devices correctly.

sections.heading: Nutrition
bullets: Adequate intake = fewer pressure injuries.
Key nutrients: protein, calories, vitamins A and C, zinc, and iron (plus adequate fluids).
Monitor weight, lymphocyte count, albumin, and hemoglobin.
Use supplements if the client is nutritionally compromised; assess intake and consult the dietitian when needed.

sections.heading: Skin hygiene
bullets: Complete a baseline risk assessment (Braden scale, etc.).
Assess skin twice daily in the hospital and weekly in home care (more often if at high risk).
Cleanse gently with mild agents; avoid hot water.
Keep skin clean, dry, and moisturized; manage moisture from incontinence, sweat, and drainage promptly.
Use barrier creams or films (dimethicone, alcohol-free sprays).
Avoid petroleum ointments, baby powder, and cornstarch.
Do not massage bony prominences or reddened areas.

sections.heading: Repositioning and avoiding trauma
bullets: Provide smooth, firm, wrinkle-free surfaces.
Use correct positioning, transferring, and turning techniques; use draw sheets or lifts — never drag the client.
Bedridden clients: keep the HOB at 30° or lower when possible to reduce shear.
Reposition bedbound clients at least every 2 hours; clients in a chair every 1 hour.
Teach clients who are able to shift weight every 15–30 minutes (commonly taught as every 15 minutes).
Positions: prone, supine, right/left lateral, right/left Sims. A 30° side tilt with pillows keeps weight off the trochanter and sacrum; avoid positioning on an existing injury.

sections.heading: Supportive devices
sections.body: Goal: keep external pressure below capillary pressure (32 mm Hg). Support surfaces reduce pressure injuries by about 60% — but they never replace turning.
bullets: Overlay mattresses — foam or gel placed on top of a standard bed.
Specialty beds — low-air-loss, high-air-loss, kinetic therapy.
Pillows, wedges, and heel protectors — offload pressure points (float the heels).
Avoid doughnut devices — they reduce blood flow and cause injury.

table.caption: Repositioning at a glance
rows: Client able to shift own weight

pearls: Reddened sacrum? Turn the client off it and reassess — never massage it and never put a doughnut under it.
Chair = every 1 hour; bed = every 2 hours; weight shift = every 15 minutes.
A specialty bed is an add-on, not a substitute for turning.
No hot water, no powder, no cornstarch — mild cleanser, pat dry, barrier cream.
redFlags: Heels resting directly on the mattress in an immobile client — float them now.
A client left sitting for hours or sliding down in bed with the HOB high — reposition now.

topics.title: The Four Stages of Pressure Injuries
topics.summary: Stage a pressure injury by the deepest tissue involved — from intact nonblanchable redness (Stage I) to damage reaching muscle or bone (Stage IV).

sections.heading: Stages I–IV
bullets: Stage I — nonblanchable erythema of intact skin, signaling potential ulceration. In people of color it appears as darkening of the skin; compare warmth, firmness, and tenderness with surrounding skin.
Stage II — partial-thickness skin loss involving the epidermis and possibly the dermis: a clear-fluid blister (intact or ruptured) or a shallow, open, pink, moist wound.
Stage III — full-thickness skin loss involving damage or necrosis of subcutaneous tissue (fat may be visible); no muscle or bone.
Stage IV — full-thickness skin loss with tissue necrosis or damage to muscle, bone, or supporting structures (e.g., tendon).

sections.heading: Recognizing stages at the bedside
bullets: Blanch test: press on a red area. If it turns white and refills, it blanches (normal response to pressure). If it stays red, it is nonblanchable — Stage I.
In darkly pigmented skin, use good lighting and rely on touch: warmth or coolness, firmness, spongy/boggy edema, and the client's report of pain.
Stage by the deepest tissue you can see or feel: fat = at least Stage III; muscle, tendon, or bone = Stage IV.
If yellow slough or black eschar covers the wound bed, treat it with the RYB color guide (cleanse yellow, debride black) and stage the wound by the deepest tissue visible.

table.caption: Quick staging comparison
rows: Nonblanchable redness; darker area in dark skin
Shallow pink moist bed or clear blister
Full thickness; fat may be visible
Bone, tendon, or muscle seen or felt

pearls: Clear blister = Stage II. Intact nonblanchable redness = Stage I.
See fat → at least Stage III. See or feel bone, tendon, or muscle → Stage IV.
Dark skin: don't wait for redness — feel for warmth, firmness, and tenderness.
redFlags: A Stage I area that does not fade after pressure is relieved — keep the client off it and update the plan.
A deep (Stage III–IV) wound with fever, increasing pain, or purulent drainage — possible infection; report to the provider.

topics.title: Pressure Injuries: The Nursing Process
topics.summary: Assess the skin and any wound the same way every time, choose the right nursing diagnoses, set measurable outcomes, carry out skin, nutrition, and teaching interventions, and revise the plan when goals are not met.

sections.heading: Assessment
bullets: Inspect the skin under good lighting, focusing on pressure areas: discoloration, abrasions, excoriations, and capillary refill/blanch response.
Palpate for temperature (↑ warmth = inflammation; ↓ coolness = poor blood flow) and edema (spongy/boggy tissue).
If an injury is present, document location, size (L × W × D), undermining, stage, wound bed color, margins, surrounding skin, drainage, signs of infection, and pain.

Measure length head-to-toe and width side-to-side in centimeters; measure depth with a sterile, moistened cotton-tipped applicator. Check for undermining (tissue destroyed beneath the intact wound edge) and note its depth and location.
Use risk tools (Braden or Norton).

sections.heading: Nursing diagnoses (slides)
bullets: Potential for impaired skin integrity (at risk, skin intact)
Impaired skin integrity
Risk for infection
Underweight
Compromised dignity
Situational low self-esteem

sections.heading: Planning — collaborative outcomes
bullets: Reposition every 2 hours (immobile clients) with positioning devices.
Mobile clients maintain or improve activity levels.
Client reports changes in skin condition (pain, redness, drainage).
Client verbalizes the importance of nutrition and hydration.
Client describes protective measures for the skin.
Well-written outcomes are client-centered, measurable, and time-limited.

sections.heading: Implementation
bullets: Skin integrity: daily skin inspection (focus on bony areas); gentle cleansing with mild agents, no hot water; moisturize dry skin; manage moisture (incontinence, sweat, drainage); avoid massage over bony prominences; proper turning, transferring, and positioning; reposition every 2 hours in bed and every 1 hour in a chair; teach weight shifting every 15 minutes.
Infection: hygiene, hydration, early recognition of signs of infection, and reporting changes to the provider.
Nutrition: assess intake, provide supplements, consult the dietitian if needed.
Teaching (clients and caregivers): risk factors, skin care and positioning, diet and hydration, dressing changes and wound care if applicable.

Delegation: UAP can turn, reposition, bathe, provide incontinence care, and report redness; the RN assesses, stages, plans, teaches, and evaluates. LPNs may perform established dressing changes on stable clients.

sections.heading: Evaluation
bullets: Reassess skin integrity daily (or more often if high risk).
Evaluate skin healing, comfort and pain control, repositioning schedule compliance, and nutritional intake.
Modify the care plan if goals are not met.
Mobile clients are instructed to report new pressure areas.

pearls: A UAP who reports a reddened area has done their job; the RN must go assess it.
Objective documentation: measurements in cm, wound bed by color and percentage, drainage type and amount — never "looks better."
Pressure injuries can affect dignity and self-esteem — acknowledge the client's feelings and plan odor and drainage control.
redFlags: A wound that is getting larger, deeper, or developing new slough, odor, or purulent drainage — reassess and revise the plan.
New confusion, fever, tachycardia, or hypotension in a client with a deep pressure injury — possible spreading infection; report immediately.

topics.title: Wound Care: RYB Color Guide & Debridement
topics.summary: Match wound care to the color of the wound bed: protect red, cleanse yellow, debride black.

sections.heading: RYB (red-yellow-black) color guide
bullets: Red — PROTECT. Clean, healthy granulation tissue (beefy red, moist, bleeds easily). Protect it from trauma and keep it moist.
Yellow — CLEANSE. Soft yellow nonviable tissue (slough). Cleanse to remove it.
Black — DEBRIDE. Thick, dry, black necrotic tissue (eschar) that must be removed for healing to occur.
In a wound with more than one color, address the least healthy tissue first (black → yellow → red).

sections.heading: Debridement methods
bullets: Sharp — surgeon with a scalpel.
Mechanical — wet-to-dry dressing. As the gauze dries it sticks to all tissue, so it also removes healthy tissue; it is not used on a clean red wound.
Chemical — enzymes applied to the necrotic tissue.
Autolytic — special dressings that capture drainage so the body's own enzymes break down dead tissue.
Maggots (biosurgery) — sterile maggots placed on nonhealing necrotic wounds digest the damaged tissue with minimal harm to healthy tissue; in some cases preferable to surgical debridement.

sections.heading: Recognizing wound infection
bullets: Signs: increased pain, redness, warmth, purulent drainage, odor, fever, and an elevated WBC.
Report changes to the provider; obtain a wound culture as prescribed before the first antibiotic dose.
Evaluate response by trending temperature, the border of redness, and the drainage.

pearls: Red = protect, yellow = cleanse, black = debride. Mixed wound? Treat the worst color first.
Never wet-to-dry a clean red wound — it pulls off the healthy tissue.
Sharp debridement = surgeon. Mechanical, chemical, and autolytic methods can be carried out by the nurse as prescribed.
Maggots eat dead tissue, not healthy tissue.
redFlags: Purulent, foul-smelling drainage with spreading redness and fever — wound infection; report and culture as prescribed.
New black eschar or increasing slough in a previously clean wound — the wound is deteriorating; revise the plan.

topics.title: Wound Healing: Types of Intention, Phases & Lifespan
topics.summary: How a wound closes (primary, secondary, or tertiary intention) and the three phases it moves through tell you which findings are expected — and which are not.

sections.heading: Types of wound healing
bullets: Primary intention — edges approximated (closed); minimal tissue loss, scarring, and granulation. Examples: surgical incision closed with sutures, staples, or adhesive closure.

Secondary intention — extensive tissue loss; edges not approximated. The wound fills in from the base with granulation tissue. Longer healing, more scarring, higher infection risk. Example: pressure injuries.
Tertiary intention (delayed primary) — wound left open 3–5 days (for edema, infection, or drainage), then closed. Greater scarring.

sections.heading: Phases of wound healing
bullets: Inflammatory (about 3 to 6 days) — Hemostasis: vessels constrict and a clot forms (scab). Phagocytosis: WBCs clean the wound (neutrophils → macrophages). Redness, edema, and exudate are normal early signs.

Proliferative (day 3 to 21) — fibroblasts make collagen → ↑ wound strength; granulation tissue forms (fragile, red, bleeds easily); epithelial cells migrate to cover the wound. In a closed incision, new collagen can be felt as a firm healing ridge.

Maturation (day 21 to 1–2 years) — collagen reorganizes and the scar strengthens, but a scar is never as strong as the original tissue. Hypertrophic scars or keloids (scar grows beyond the wound edges; more common in people with darker skin) may form.

sections.heading: Lifespan considerations
bullets: Older adults — slower inflammatory response, slower epithelialization, thinner and more fragile skin, and a blunted fever response. Infection may first appear as new confusion, a small rise from baseline temperature, or loss of appetite.
Handle older skin gently (lift with draw sheets) to prevent skin tears.

table.caption: Phases at a glance
rows: Fibroblasts make collagen; granulation; epithelial migration
Beefy red, fragile granulation; healing ridge; edges covering
Scar fades; never as strong as original tissue; possible keloid

pearls: Mild redness and swelling along an incision on postop day 1–2 is expected inflammation; increasing redness, pain, and purulent drainage on day 4–5 suggests infection.
Granulation tissue should be beefy red and moist and bleed easily; pale or dry tissue suggests poor healing.
No healing ridge by about day 9 suggests weak collagen and a higher risk of dehiscence.
Secondary intention = open, fills from the bottom, slower, more scarring, higher infection risk.
redFlags: Separated edges on a primary-intention incision — possible dehiscence.
New confusion or a low-grade temperature rise in an older adult with a wound — possible infection.

topics.title: Health Promotion, Factors Affecting Healing & Exudate Types
topics.summary: Healing needs oxygen, nutrients, and a clean wound. Nutrition, exercise, and not smoking help; malnutrition, obesity, smoking, diabetes, and certain drugs slow it down. Drainage type tells you what is happening in the wound.

sections.heading: Health promotion in wound healing
bullets: Nutrition: ↑ protein, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins A and C, iron, zinc, and copper. Malnutrition and obesity both delay healing.
Lifestyle: exercise → better circulation and faster healing; smoking → ↓ oxygen delivery and slower healing (nicotine constricts vessels; carbon monoxide displaces oxygen on hemoglobin).
Medications: steroids, aspirin, and chemotherapy impair healing; long-term antibiotics → resistant infections.
Other factors: advanced age and chronic conditions such as diabetes (high glucose impairs WBC function; vascular disease reduces blood flow).

sections.heading: Exudate types
bullets: Serous — clear, watery, straw-colored; mild inflammation (e.g., blister fluid).
Purulent — thick, opaque, milky; pus = WBCs + debris; may be yellow, green, or blue; indicates infection.
Sanguineous (hemorrhagic) — bright or dark red; indicates capillary damage and bleeding.
Serosanguineous — clear plus blood-tinged; common in surgical incisions.
Purosanguineous — pus plus blood; seen in infected wounds.

sections.heading: Culturally competent care
bullets: Explore the client's beliefs and practices (e.g., religious fasting, dietary customs) and collaborate on adjustments to meals and medications that protect healing while respecting the client's values.

pearls: Both malnutrition AND obesity impair healing.
Steroids, aspirin, and chemotherapy slow healing; long-term antibiotics breed resistant infections.
Vaping still delivers nicotine — it still constricts vessels.
Expected postop drainage: sanguineous → serosanguineous → serous, decreasing in amount. Going back to bright red, or turning purulent, needs reporting.
redFlags: Purulent or purosanguineous drainage with fever — wound infection; report to the provider.
Persistently high blood glucose in a client with a wound — report for treatment adjustment.

topics.title: Wound Complications: Hemorrhage, Infection, Dehiscence & Evisceration
topics.summary: Know when each complication is most likely, what it looks like, and the first thing to do — especially for evisceration, a surgical emergency.

sections.heading: Hemorrhage
bullets: Abnormal bleeding; can result from a slipped stitch, a dislodged clot, or erosion of a vessel.
Greatest risk: the first 48 hours after surgery.
External: saturated dressing with bright red blood. Internal: swelling, distention, hematoma — the dressing may be dry.
Signs of volume loss: restlessness, tachycardia, falling BP, cool clammy skin, ↓ urine output, falling hemoglobin.
Actions: apply pressure to external bleeding, monitor vital signs, notify the surgeon promptly.

sections.heading: Infection
bullets: Signs: ↑ pain, redness, drainage, odor, fever, ↑ WBC.
Higher risk: immunocompromised clients, contaminated wounds, and GI surgery.
Actions: report to the surgeon, obtain cultures as prescribed, give antibiotics as prescribed, and support healing (glucose control, nutrition).

sections.heading: Dehiscence
bullets: Wound reopening (separation of the wound layers), most often in abdominal wounds.
Client reports a "popping" sensation after coughing or sneezing; often a sudden gush of serosanguineous drainage.
Risk factors include obesity, malnutrition, infection, steroids, and strain (coughing, vomiting, lifting).
Actions: low Fowler's with knees bent, cover with a sterile saline-moistened dressing, notify the surgeon.

sections.heading: Evisceration — surgical emergency
bullets: Protrusion of organs through the incision.
Stay with the client and call for help; cover with sterile normal saline–moistened dressings; position with knees bent; notify the surgeon. Never push the organs back in.
Monitor for shock, keep the client NPO, and prepare for surgery.

sections.heading: Preventing complications
bullets: Teach the client to splint the incision with a pillow when coughing, sneezing, or deep breathing.
Avoid heavy lifting and straining (stool softeners and fluids as prescribed); use an abdominal binder if prescribed.
Promote nutrition, glucose control, and activity; teach signs of infection, bleeding, and separation to report.

table.caption: Complications: key signs and priority action
rows: Bright red drainage or swelling/hematoma; tachycardia, falling BP
Pressure on external bleeding, vital signs, notify surgeon
↑ pain, redness, purulent drainage, odor, fever, ↑ WBC
Report; culture and antibiotics as prescribed
Low Fowler's knees bent, sterile moist saline dressing, notify surgeon
Stay, call for help, sterile NS dressings, knees bent, notify surgeon

pearls: Evisceration: stay, saline-moist sterile cover, knees bent, surgeon — never push organs back in.
"I felt something pop when I coughed" → assess the incision at the bedside now.
A dry dressing does not rule out bleeding — look for swelling, distention, tachycardia, and restlessness.
Splinting reduces tension on the suture line during coughing and deep breathing.
redFlags: Organs visible through the incision — surgical emergency.
Postop tachycardia, falling BP, and a tense, swelling incision area — internal hemorrhage.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A 79-year-old client is on bed rest after hip fracture repair. The client responds only to painful stimuli, eats about one-third of meals, is often incontinent of urine, and slides down in bed when the head of the bed is raised. The Braden scale total is 11. The skin is intact, and the reddened areas over the sacrum and heels blanch and fade after turning. Which action is the nurse's priority?
options: Document a Stage 1 pressure injury over the sacrum and both heels
Turn at least every 2 hours on a pressure-redistribution surface
Recheck the Braden score in 1 week because the total shows mild risk
Massage the reddened sacrum and heels at each turn to restore flow
optionRationales: Incorrect. Redness that blanches and fades after turning is normal reactive redness, not a Stage 1 injury; the skin is still intact and undamaged.

Correct. A Braden total of 11 means high risk (lower score = higher risk) while the skin is still intact, so the priority is prevention: relieve pressure at least every 2 hours and spread the load with a support surface.
Incorrect. A total of 10–12 is high risk, not mild; waiting a week ignores a client whose every subscale is pulling the score down.
Incorrect. Massage over bony prominences is avoided because it can break fragile capillaries and worsen deep tissue damage.
questions.rationale: Three pieces connect here. The Braden scale runs 6–23 and is inverse, so 11 is high risk. The skin is intact and the redness blanches, so there is no injury yet — the nursing diagnosis is potential for impaired skin integrity, not impaired skin integrity. For a high-risk client with intact skin, the priority intervention is prevention: reposition at least every 2 hours and use a pressure-redistribution surface to keep interface pressure below capillary pressure.
questions.takeaway: Low Braden score + intact, blanching skin = high risk with no injury yet → prevent: turn q2h on a support surface.
questions.hintContent: Recall which direction the Braden scale runs, what blanching redness means, and the repositioning interval for a bedbound client.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide first whether an injury exists or only risk; then pick the action that matches that conclusion and the size of the risk.
